Medicine.question: ১) The term ‘peptic ulcer’ refers to an ulcer in any of the following region except.....?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is distal ileum. Crohn’s disease can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract from mouth to anus, but the terminal (distal) ileum is the most commonly affected site. It commonly involves the ileocaecal region.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Proximal ileum – Less commonly involved compared with terminal ileum.
  • Proximal jejunum – Jejunal involvement can occur but is uncommon.
  • Distal jejunum – May be involved in rare cases but is not the typical site.

High-yield points:

  • Crohn’s disease → Terminal ileum + ileocaecal region (most common)
  • Crohn’s → Transmural inflammation + skip lesions + non-caseating granuloma
  • Ulcerative colitis → Colon only + continuous mucosal inflammation
  • Crohn’s complications → Strictures, fistula, abscess, malabsorption (B12 deficiency)

Medicine.question: ২) Which is not true about NUD?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is males are more affected. Non-ulcer dyspepsia (NUD), also called functional dyspepsia, is a chronic disorder characterized by dyspeptic symptoms without any identifiable organic disease. It is actually more common in females than males.

The other options are true:

  • Chronic condition – True. NUD is a long-standing functional gastrointestinal disorder with recurrent symptoms.

  • Without any organic cause – True. Endoscopy and investigations do not reveal an organic cause such as peptic ulcer, malignancy, or inflammation.

  • Usually common in young patient – True. Functional dyspepsia commonly affects younger individuals, although it can occur at any age.

High-yield points:

  • NUD = Functional dyspepsia

  • Symptoms → Epigastric pain, early satiety, postprandial fullness, bloating

  • No structural abnormality on endoscopy

  • More common in females

  • Alarm features → Weight loss, bleeding, anaemia, dysphagia → investigate for organic disease

Medicine.question: ৩) Gastric erosions & ulcers are differentiated from each other on the basis of their penetration into.......?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is muscularis mucosa. The distinction between a gastric erosion and a gastric ulcer is based on the depth of mucosal injury.

  • Gastric erosion → A superficial mucosal defect that does not penetrate beyond the muscularis mucosa.

  • Gastric ulcer → A deeper defect that extends through the muscularis mucosa into the submucosa or deeper layers.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Muscularis interna – Not a standard layer used for differentiating erosion and ulcer.

  • Muscularis externa – A deeper muscular layer involved in gastrointestinal motility; ulcers may penetrate it in complicated cases.

  • Submucosa – Ulcers extend into the submucosa, but the key dividing point is whether the lesion crosses the muscularis mucosa.

High-yield points:

  • Erosion → Mucosal defect only, does NOT cross muscularis mucosa

  • Ulcer → Defect extends beyond muscularis mucosa

  • Muscularis mucosa = key boundary between erosion and ulcer

  • Peptic ulcer complications → Bleeding, perforation, penetration, gastric outlet obstruction

Medicine.question: ৪) Which part of intestine is commonly affected in Crohn's disease?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is distal ileum. Crohn’s disease can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract from mouth to anus, but the terminal (distal) ileum is the most commonly affected site. It commonly involves the ileocaecal region.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Proximal ileum – Less commonly involved compared with terminal ileum.
  • Proximal jejunum – Jejunal involvement can occur but is uncommon.
  • Distal jejunum – May be involved in rare cases but is not the typical site.

High-yield points:

  • Crohn’s disease → Terminal ileum + ileocaecal region (most common)
  • Crohn’s → Transmural inflammation + skip lesions + non-caseating granuloma
  • Ulcerative colitis → Colon only + continuous mucosal inflammation
  • Crohn’s complications → Strictures, fistula, abscess, malabsorption (B12 deficiency)

Medicine.question: ৫) Which is one of the invasive methods for the diagnosis of Helicobacter pylori infection?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is rapid urease test. It is an invasive method for diagnosing Helicobacter pylori infection because it requires upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with gastric biopsy. The biopsy sample is tested for urease activity produced by H. pylori, which converts urea into ammonia and raises the pH.

The other options are incorrect because they are non-invasive methods:

  • Serology – Detects antibodies against H. pylori in blood; does not require endoscopy.

  • Faecal antigen test – Detects H. pylori antigen in stool; useful for diagnosis and confirmation of eradication.

  • C-13 urea breath test – Detects urease activity by measuring labelled carbon dioxide after ingestion of labelled urea; non-invasive and highly accurate.

High-yield points:

  • Invasive H. pylori tests:

    • Rapid urease test (RUT)

    • Histology of gastric biopsy

    • Culture

  • Non-invasive H. pylori tests:

    • Urea breath test (C-13/C-14)

    • Stool antigen test

    • Serology

  • Best test for eradication confirmation → Urea breath test or stool antigen test

  • Rapid urease test → Requires endoscopy + biopsy

Medicine.question: ৬) Which operation protects ulcerative colitis but increases the risk of Crohn's disease?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is appendicectomy. Previous appendicectomy, especially when performed early in life, is associated with a reduced risk of developing ulcerative colitis (UC). However, some studies suggest that appendicectomy may be associated with an increased likelihood of Crohn’s disease (CD) diagnosis, possibly because appendicectomy may be performed in patients whose early Crohn’s disease was misdiagnosed as appendicitis.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Cholecystectomy – Not known to protect against ulcerative colitis or increase Crohn’s disease risk.

  • Ileostomy – A surgical procedure used in management of severe UC or Crohn’s disease; it does not have a protective role against UC.

  • Colostomy – Used in selected colorectal conditions; not associated with altering UC or Crohn’s disease risk.

High-yield points:

  • Appendicectomy → ↓ Risk of ulcerative colitis

  • Smoking → ↓ Risk of UC but ↑ Risk of Crohn’s disease

  • Crohn’s disease → Skip lesions + transmural inflammation

  • Ulcerative colitis → Continuous mucosal inflammation starting from rectum

Medicine.question: ৭) What is the indications for emergency surgery in peptic ulcer disease??
Medicine.option4: Persistent ulceration despite adequate medical therapy
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is perforation. In peptic ulcer disease (PUD), emergency surgery is indicated mainly for acute complications that are life-threatening, especially perforation, which leads to leakage of gastric/duodenal contents into the peritoneal cavity causing peritonitis.

The other options are incorrect because they are usually elective surgical indications:

  • Gastric outflow obstruction – Causes persistent vomiting and gastric retention; surgery may be required, but it is generally an elective procedure after correction of fluid and electrolyte imbalance.

  • Recurrent ulcer following gastric surgery – May require revision surgery, but it is not an emergency indication.

  • Persistent ulceration despite adequate medical therapy – May require elective surgery if complications or malignancy suspicion exists, but not an emergency.

High-yield points:

  • Emergency surgery in PUD → Perforation + uncontrolled bleeding

  • Common PUD complications:

    • Haemorrhage (most common)

    • Perforation

    • Gastric outlet obstruction

    • Penetration

  • Perforated peptic ulcer → Sudden severe abdominal pain + rigid abdomen + free air under diaphragm on X-ray

Medicine.question: ৮) Which is pathognomonic radiological sign of Crohn's disease ?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is string sign. The string sign of Kantor is a classic radiological feature of Crohn’s disease, caused by marked narrowing of the terminal ileum due to transmural inflammation, oedema, and fibrosis. A thin stream of barium passes through the narrowed segment, producing a "string-like" appearance.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Whirlpool sign – Seen in intestinal volvulus due to twisting of bowel and mesenteric vessels.

  • Ribbon sign – Associated with malabsorption syndromes, especially coeliac disease, due to a narrow column of barium.

  • Double bubble sign – Seen in duodenal atresia, showing dilatation of stomach and proximal duodenum.

High-yield points:

  • Crohn’s disease → String sign (terminal ileum)

  • Crohn’s radiology → Skip lesions, strictures, fistulae, cobblestone appearance

  • Ulcerative colitis → Lead pipe colon

  • Coeliac disease → Ribbon sign

  • Volvulus → Whirlpool sign

Medicine.question: ৯) Which is not one of the characteristic triad of Zollinger–Ellison syndrome?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is heals with PPI. The classic triad of Zollinger–Ellison syndrome (ZES) includes:

  1. Gastrinoma (usually a pancreatic or duodenal neuroendocrine tumour)

  2. Gastric acid hypersecretion due to excessive gastrin secretion

  3. Severe/recurrent peptic ulceration

Although proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) are highly effective in controlling acid secretion and symptoms in ZES, healing with PPI is not part of the characteristic triad.

The other options are true features:

  • Severe peptic ulceration – True; ulcers are often multiple, recurrent, and may occur in unusual sites.

  • Gastric acid hypersecretion – True; gastrin stimulates parietal cells causing marked acid production.

  • Gastrinoma – True; the underlying tumour secretes excessive gastrin.

High-yield points:

  • Zollinger–Ellison syndrome = Gastrinoma → ↑ Gastrin → ↑ Gastric acid → Multiple recurrent ulcers

  • Common association → MEN 1 syndrome

  • Treatment → High-dose PPI

  • PPI controls acid secretion but is not a diagnostic triad component

Medicine.question: ১০) Which layer of colon is involved in ulcerative colitis?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is mucosa. Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease that primarily affects the colonic mucosa and submucosa. The inflammation is continuous, starting from the rectum and extending proximally.

The inflammation in UC is usually limited to the mucosa, unlike Crohn’s disease, which involves the entire thickness of the bowel wall.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Submucosa – May be involved due to extension of inflammation, but the primary site is the mucosa.

  • Muscle layer – Usually spared in UC; involvement is more characteristic of transmural diseases like Crohn’s disease.

  • Serosa – Not typically involved in UC.

High-yield points:

  • Ulcerative colitis → Mucosa + submucosa

  • Crohn’s disease → Transmural inflammation (all layers)

  • UC → Continuous lesions starting from rectum

  • Crohn’s → Skip lesions + fistula + stricture

Medicine.question: ১১) What is the commonest site of gastric ulcer & duodenal ulcer?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is lesser curvature of stomach and first part of duodenum.

  • Gastric ulcer most commonly occurs along the lesser curvature of the stomach, especially near the incisura angularis, due to the concentration of acid exposure and mucosal vulnerability.

  • Duodenal ulcer most commonly occurs in the first part of the duodenum (duodenal bulb), just beyond the pylorus, because it is exposed to acidic gastric contents.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Greater curvature & 2nd part – Not typical sites for peptic ulcers.

  • Lesser curvature & 2nd part – Gastric site is correct, but duodenal ulcers are most common in the first part, not second part.

  • Greater curvature & 1st part – Duodenal site is correct, but gastric ulcers rarely occur on the greater curvature.

High-yield points:

  • Gastric ulcer → Lesser curvature (near incisura angularis)

  • Duodenal ulcer → First part of duodenum (duodenal bulb)

  • Gastric ulcer → Pain worsens with meals

  • Duodenal ulcer → Pain relieved by meals

  • Commonest cause of both → H. pylori infection + NSAIDs

Medicine.question: ১২) Crohn's disease is more common in....?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is smokers. Cigarette smoking is an important environmental risk factor for Crohn’s disease (CD). Smoking increases the risk of developing Crohn’s disease, increases disease severity, and is associated with more frequent relapses and complications.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Non-smokers – Have a lower risk compared with smokers.

  • Ex-smokers – Stopping smoking reduces the risk and improves the course of Crohn’s disease, although previous exposure may still influence disease risk.

  • Passive smokers – Passive smoke exposure is not a major established risk factor for Crohn’s disease.

High-yield points:

  • Smoking → ↑ Crohn’s disease risk and severity

  • Smoking → ↓ Risk of ulcerative colitis (UC)

  • Crohn’s disease → Transmural inflammation + skip lesions + fistula

  • Ulcerative colitis → Continuous mucosal inflammation

Medicine.question: ১৩) What is the nature of pain in PUD?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is burning. The pain of peptic ulcer disease (PUD) is classically described as a burning or gnawing epigastric pain due to irritation of the gastric or duodenal mucosa by acid and pepsin.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Spasmodic pain – Usually associated with hollow organ obstruction or muscular contraction, not typical of PUD.

  • Colicky pain – Characteristic of intermittent obstruction of tubular organs, such as biliary colic or renal colic.

  • Throbbing pain – Usually associated with vascular or inflammatory conditions.

High-yield points:

  • PUD pain → Burning/gnawing epigastric pain

  • Duodenal ulcer → Pain relieved by food, occurs 2–5 hours after meals or at night

  • Gastric ulcer → Pain worsens with meals

  • PUD major causes → H. pylori + NSAIDs

Medicine.question: ১৪) Recurrent abdominal pain in association with abnormal defecation in the absence of a structural abnormality of the gut is called........?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is IBS (Irritable bowel syndrome). IBS is a functional gastrointestinal disorder characterized by recurrent abdominal pain associated with altered bowel habits (diarrhoea, constipation, or both) without any structural abnormality of the gut.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • IBD (Inflammatory bowel disease) – Includes Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis, which cause structural inflammation and mucosal damage in the gastrointestinal tract.

  • PUD (Peptic ulcer disease) – Causes mucosal ulceration in the stomach or duodenum, usually presenting with epigastric pain.

  • PID (Pelvic inflammatory disease) – Infection/inflammation of female pelvic organs and is unrelated to functional bowel symptoms.

High-yield points:

  • IBS → Abdominal pain + altered bowel habit + no structural abnormality

  • IBS diagnosis → Rome IV criteria

  • IBD → Inflammation + structural bowel damage

  • IBS alarm features → Weight loss, bleeding, anaemia, nocturnal symptoms → investigate for organic disease

Medicine.question: ১৫) Persistent daily vomiting in PUD suggests.....?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is gastric outlet obstruction. Persistent daily vomiting in a patient with peptic ulcer disease (PUD) suggests obstruction at the pylorus or duodenum, usually due to chronic duodenal ulcer causing scarring and fibrosis. This prevents gastric emptying and leads to recurrent vomiting.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Perforation – Causes sudden severe abdominal pain, rigid abdomen, and peritonitis rather than persistent daily vomiting.

  • Ca stomach (gastric carcinoma) – Can cause vomiting due to obstruction, but in a known PUD patient, persistent vomiting classically suggests gastric outlet obstruction.

  • Small bowel syndrome – Not a typical complication of PUD.

High-yield points:

  • PUD complications:

    1. Bleeding (most common)

    2. Perforation

    3. Gastric outlet obstruction

    4. Penetration

  • Gastric outlet obstruction features:

    • Persistent vomiting

    • Early satiety

    • Weight loss

    • Succussion splash

    • Visible gastric peristalsis

  • Chronic duodenal ulcer → Fibrosis → Pyloric/duodenal narrowing → Obstruction

Medicine.question: ১৬) Which is one of the alarming features of IBS?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is rectal bleeding. Rectal bleeding is an alarm feature in a patient with suspected irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) because IBS is a functional gastrointestinal disorder and should not cause bleeding. The presence of bleeding suggests an organic pathology such as inflammatory bowel disease, colorectal cancer, or other gastrointestinal disorders and requires further evaluation.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Dyspepsia – May coexist with IBS (functional dyspepsia overlap) and is not considered an alarm feature.

  • Weight gain – Not an alarm feature; IBS may be associated with normal weight changes.

  • Jaundice – Not a typical alarm feature of IBS and suggests hepatobiliary disease rather than intestinal pathology.

High-yield points:

IBS alarm features (suggest organic disease):

  • Rectal bleeding

  • Unintentional weight loss

  • Iron deficiency anaemia

  • Nocturnal symptoms

  • Fever

  • Family history of colorectal cancer/IBD

  • New onset symptoms at older age

IBS → Abdominal pain + altered bowel habit + no structural abnormality

Medicine.question: ১৭) Which is the preferred investigation in PUD?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is endoscopy (upper gastrointestinal endoscopy/OGD). Endoscopy is the preferred investigation in peptic ulcer disease (PUD) because it allows direct visualization of the ulcer, assessment of severity, detection of complications, and biopsy to exclude malignancy (especially in gastric ulcers).

The other options are incorrect because:

  • USG of whole abdomen – Has limited value in diagnosing PUD; it is not useful for visualizing gastric or duodenal mucosal ulcers.

  • Barium meal X-ray – Previously used for diagnosis of peptic ulcers but is less preferred now because it cannot provide tissue biopsy and may miss small lesions.

  • CT scan – Not a routine investigation for uncomplicated PUD; mainly used for complications such as perforation or malignancy staging.

High-yield points:

  • PUD investigation of choice → Upper GI endoscopy

  • Endoscopy advantages:

    • Direct visualization

    • Biopsy of gastric ulcer

    • Detection of bleeding lesions

  • H. pylori diagnosis during endoscopy → Rapid urease test, histology, culture

  • Gastric ulcer → Always consider biopsy to exclude malignancy

Medicine.question: ১৮) PUD is closely associated with......?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori). H. pylori infection is one of the major causes of peptic ulcer disease (PUD). It colonizes the gastric mucosa and causes chronic gastritis, leading to impaired mucosal defence and increased susceptibility to acid-related injury.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Campylobacter jejuni (C. jejuni) – Causes acute gastroenteritis, especially diarrhoea, and is associated with Guillain–Barré syndrome, not PUD.

  • E. coli – Causes various intestinal infections (e.g., diarrhoea, UTI), but is not a cause of PUD.

  • B. coli (Balantidium coli) – Causes intestinal infection/colitis, not peptic ulcer disease.

High-yield points:

  • Major causes of PUD:

    1. H. pylori infection

    2. NSAIDs

  • H. pylori complications:

    • Peptic ulcer disease

    • Gastric adenocarcinoma

    • Gastric MALT lymphoma

  • H. pylori → Urease positive, gram-negative curved bacillus

  • Most common site of H. pylori colonization → Gastric antrum

Medicine.question: ১৯) Which is not true about duodenal ulcer?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is more chance of hematemesis. Duodenal ulcer can cause upper gastrointestinal bleeding, but melena is more common than hematemesis because bleeding from the duodenum usually passes through the intestine before appearing as stool. Hematemesis is more commonly associated with gastric or oesophageal bleeding.

The other options are true about duodenal ulcer:

  • Periodicity present – True. Duodenal ulcer pain often shows a periodic pattern with symptom-free intervals and recurrence.

  • Appetite good – True. Patients with duodenal ulcer usually maintain appetite and may experience relief of pain after eating.

  • More in empty stomach – True. Duodenal ulcer pain typically occurs when the stomach is empty, usually 2–5 hours after meals or at night, and improves after food intake.

High-yield points:

  • Duodenal ulcer:

    • Pain occurs on empty stomach / night pain

    • Pain relieved by food

    • Appetite usually good

    • Common site → First part of duodenum

  • Gastric ulcer:

    • Pain worsens after meals

    • Appetite may decrease due to fear of pain

  • Duodenal ulcer bleeding → Melena more common than hematemesis

Medicine.question: ২০) Which one is gold standard for H. pylori?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is microscopic culture. Culture of H. pylori from gastric biopsy is considered the gold standard because it provides direct evidence of infection and allows antibiotic sensitivity testing.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Rapid urease test – A highly useful invasive test performed on gastric biopsy. It is rapid and commonly used during endoscopy but is not the gold standard.

  • Urea breath test – A highly accurate non-invasive test and preferred for confirming eradication after treatment, but not the gold standard.

  • Serology – Detects antibodies against H. pylori. It cannot distinguish between active and previous infection.

High-yield points:

  • Gold standard for H. pylori diagnosis → Culture from gastric biopsy

  • Most commonly used invasive test → Rapid urease test

  • Best non-invasive test → Urea breath test

  • Eradication confirmation → Urea breath test / stool antigen test

  • H. pylori → Urease positive, gram-negative curved bacillus
